utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters, counsel of the Prosecution, the counsel for the Defence, and the accused. We shall continue, without further delay, with the examination, Mr. Registrar, of a whole series of exhibits which have not been admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. They're either exhibits that have not been tendered and some that have not been admitted. Some were pending before the testimony of the accused, and then there are all the exhibits presented since the 17th of February, during the testimony of General Blaskic. Are there any pending since the beginning of the Blaskic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Since the beginning decisions were regularly taken by the Chamber regarding exhibits, and there are only a few, a few rare ones, on which the parties may have to express themselves today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps the Prosecutor would like to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Last night Mr. Kehoe and I reviewed the exhibits. We had conversations with Defence counsel. We have been able to narrow significantly the differences that we may have and there will be only a few items that are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You would like us to adjourn straightaway perhaps, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be wonderful. I can identify, first, Mr. President, the items that the Prosecutor objects to, and if I give you that list then let me begin and then counsel can identify the list that he has issues about and then we can proceed from there. The Prosecutor objects to Defence Exhibit 89, 92, 119, 120, 127, 128, 129, 197, and 590, and in respect of Defence Exhibit 591, which is a large red binder with numerous tabs, we object to certain items within Defence Exhibit 591. Those are found at tabs 36, 37, 38, 176, 177, and 178. In respect of Defence Exhibit 588, we object to certain conclusions found in the index in respect of documents that are found at tab number 26, 27, and 33, although we do not object to the documents themselves. It's our conclusion that the index is not accurate in its conclusions in respect of those documents. So those, Mr. President, represent the sum total of the exhibits to which we object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, would you like me to respond to this list of objected to Defence Exhibits or simply give you, at this juncture, the list of Prosecution exhibits to which we the Defence object or both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we'll have to do both. The Prosecutor has just given you a list of Defence exhibits to which he is objecting, objecting to their admission, and I think you could do the same. I haven't taken notes, but I think the registrar has, so you could do the same thing, Mr. Hayman. First give us a list of exhibits which will give me an idea of the work ahead and then you yourself can make your statements. Do you have many Prosecution Exhibits that you are objecting to their admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Six plus a category of exhibits, Mr. President, so, in effect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Certain categories. I understand the nuance, but we'll see. So let's hear the first six exhibits you're objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 41. That's a letter from President Izetbegovic. Prosecutor's Exhibits 154 and 155, which are news articles relating to the testimony, which I believe was in open session, of Mr. Ashdown, and the napkin incident at the Whitehall banquet, if the Court recalls the napkin incident. Prosecutor's Exhibit 443 which was a videotape, and I recall there was a problem with the date. I believe Mr. Kehoe was going to get back to the court as to the date of that tape which may, in fact, be a BBC broadcast. Prosecutor's Exhibit 566, which I understand is to be withdrawn, and I understand Prosecutor's Exhibit 41 is to be withdrawn as well, Mr. President, so that's two which may not bear or need further discussion. Prosecutor's Exhibit 666 is the order from January 1993 from Milivoj Petkovic attaching the Vitezovi to Colonel Blaskic. Colonel Blaskic did not recognise or authenticate the document, and the Defence objects to it unless we're told with greater specificity where it came from. At the time it was offered, we were told that it was obtained from the Croat side of the Bosnian-Herzegovinan federation by a Dutch peacekeeper, and we seek further information, Mr. President, concerning whether the -- no arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, don't argue, please, Mr. Hayman. I don't have the elements, nor do my colleagues, but it's just to have an idea of the exhibits first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. Our objection to that is conditional, if you will. If that information is provided to the Court, we wouldn't have an objection to it. Lastly, we have an objection to the various documents that have been produced as a result of searches, search warrants, executed for a reason I can explain or if the Court wishes to hear that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Registrar, would you like to suggest a method of work for us or shall I do that? What are your feelings? You have experience with such debates. I don't have any particular experience as I come from a slightly different system. Perhaps Judge Rodrigues can help. Perhaps we collect the exhibits and then discuss their weight, but the question of admission first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would propose that we review all the exhibits up to the 17th of February, that is, the beginning of General Blaskic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well then. The first stage, the exhibits as far as the 17th of February, up to the 17th of February. Let us begin with the Prosecutor who objects to Defence Exhibits. The first exhibit please, Mr. Prosecutor. The exhibits up to the 17th of February. That is the first stage. I see you have taken a note of them. (Trial Chamber confers with registrar)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. In that case, we're going to proceed as follows, so that my colleagues and I can do our work properly: For the moment, we're going to discuss the admission of exhibits to which there are objections either by the Prosecutor or the Defence up to the 17th of February, the beginning of the hearing of General Blaskic as a witness. Thanks to the registrar, we will begin with the first exhibit that the Prosecutor objects to, and that appears to be Exhibit 89, D89. For the benefit of my colleagues, which is the one that comes next?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "NA" means that the exhibit was not admitted on the 27th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. It was not admitted on the 25th of February, it was a protected witness, Witness HH, and can I say this in public, Mr. Registrar or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The list cannot provide any real information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, we don't have to have a closed session, but you will let me know when that is necessary. So D89 is a Defence exhibit tendered during the testimony of Witness HH. It is a list of men who were given work to do in connection with the artillery and this list contains their responsibilities and their functions. Mr. Prosecutor, why do you object to this exhibit being admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object because this is an exhibit that the Court has already ruled on. I refer the Chamber to page 6942, and I will quote Your Honour, Mr. President, at lines 11 through 15 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm afraid of that. But go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of this particular exhibit, Your Honour stated: "JUDGE JORDA: The Judges have decided that the document was not identified by the witness. The document was not identified by the witness and he does not recognise this, and therefore, the document cannot be accepted as an exhibit." That is the basis of our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is the basis of a decision that we took, my dear colleagues; the question of identification by the witness. In that case, we took that decision some time ago. So, Mr. Hayman, are you opposing this observation? This need not be my definitive decision, but we can decide on the bench about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This list, Mr. President, as I understand it, it's a list of artillery personnel, the so-called light artillery division. I think that since the Court's ruling, there has been concrete identification of at least some of these individuals, including the first individual at the top of page 1, Mirko Batinic, as the commander of the division. So some of the information in the document has been confirmed by subsequent testimony. The other reason I'm concerned that it needs to be part of the record is, as I recall, this was shown to a witness who identified the commander of the Operative Zone level light artillery group as someone other than Mr. Batinic. This document was then shown to the witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This document was shown to the witness, and the witness said, "No, I don't recognise any of these people as having anything to do with the light artillery division." I'm paraphrasing and I'm going from memory, Mr. President, because I haven't found this passage or exchange in the transcript, and if I make an error, I invite correction. But it seems to me, for the record to be complete, since a witness was shown this document, the witness was asked, did he recognise names on the document? The witness said no. That's my recollection; but it was a long time ago. That for the record to be complete, it needs to be in the record. I have no problem with the Court noting that this document has not been authenticated. The Defence concedes that it hasn't been authenticated other than by certain corroborating information, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: [redacted] I only read the first part of your ruling. I can continue with the rest of your ruling. I thought the first part would be dispositive. I think it's important, however, that the Court consider that the Defence must -- I'm sorry, let me retract that. Let me continue with your ruling. I read the first part of your ruling which was the decision. The second part of your ruling went on to say: "JUDGE JORDA: In the second place, it is legitimate for Mr. Nobilo to question the witness on points that interest him using a document, whether it is given directly to him or whether Mr. Nobilo considers it as something which is his own documentation. "Third, if the Defence wants to tender this as an exhibit after the cross-examination of the witness on the specific point, at that point the Defence must provide the Trial Chamber with all the elements which allow it to identify and to authenticate it so the Prosecutor can exercise his own right for a redirect." Our view, Mr. President, is that there was a clear ruling on this document, the witness could not identify this document, and we therefore object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is true. But I thought that Mr. Hayman was saying that certain parts of that document were authenticated through other witnesses. That is what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if Mr. Hayman wants to direct me to testimony in the transcript where another witness identified and authenticated this document, then we would reconsider our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am in a more flexible system -- I am saying this in passing -- because it is true, in my system, the exhibit would be admitted, and then the Judges would assess it as having limited value because it was challenged. Personally, my tendency would be to admit it, in view of what Mr. Hayman told us, saying that certain aspects of it were authenticated by other witnesses. Could we perhaps find a practical solution, I turn to the registrar, of the type -- but, of course, I will need the approval of my colleagues -- the admission but with the addition of the record, the transcript from this morning, saying that certain parts were authenticated and others not. Before I consult my colleagues, Mr. Hayman, do you have other observations to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I see, Mr. President, that General Blaskic identified Mirko Batinic as a member of the Operative Zone command at page 19321 of the transcript. He wasn't shown the document, and it doesn't appear to be more specific than that. That's the only passage I can quickly find where the identity of this person was confirmed, but only partially. And I'm not saying that the document itself was authenticated by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could a partial admission be acceptable, but asking the registrar to take note of the points made by the Defence and the Prosecution, that it hasn't been fully authenticated?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make an observation on your observation? That is, we don't care to be hypertechnical in terms of the admission of these documents. We would accept your proposal, Mr. President, that the objections be noted by both sides, we articulate what our objections are, and the Court take these documents into evidence, noting what the objections are from both sides, and give them whatever weight it deems appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then it would be a partial admission, according to the procedural system that we are familiar with, a partial admission with this addition of the comments made today, that is, partial recognition of some elements specifically by the accused. But I must consult my colleagues because they probably know this procedural system better than I. Mr. Hayman -- thank you, Judge Rodrigues -- you want to respond to the proposal of the Prosecution? No objection? Then let me consult my colleagues, please. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, my dear colleagues. So that is how we are going to proceed. Take note, Mr. Registrar, of this admission, but a partial admission, with the reservations noted and all the possibilities will be open, so should there be an appeal, that we will have a record of it all. Thank you. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's acceptable. Let me just make sure in my own mind that a partial admission means that the piece of evidence that is being submitted will be considered by the Judges. Depending on weight that the Court gives it, it could well conclude that it is worthy of full weight or it could reject, in its own deliberations, the piece of evidence. That is how I understand what you're saying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is to say, the elements of the exhibit which have been authenticated today are fully admitted. That is what I would call a partial admission. If, of course, the Judges find in the exhibit elements in support of their conviction, then I think they should say in their ruling that they gave it certain weight but taking into account that it hadn't been admitted. Of course, the Judges will be exposed to the possibility of appeal. So when using that exhibit, the Judges must use only those parts of the exhibit that have been authenticated. Then, of course, it is up to the Judges to give them the weight they deem fit. Are we agreed? Would you like to join in this debate? If the Judges use this exhibit, they must take into account all these observations made and have a debate amongst themselves in the case of any difficulty. Are we agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor agrees, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The next piece of evidence is Exhibit 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, D92. It was not admitted on the 25th of February, again with the Witness HH. For the benefit of my colleagues, I think we can speak of what it was about. It is a statement, I will not say by whom because the person is under anonymity, made in Vitez on the 7th of February, 1993, giving the reasons why he abandoned his post. I will not say more because it will permit identification and we're in public session. Mr. Prosecutor, it is an exhibit tendered on the 25th of February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I would direct the Chamber's attention to the transcript, English version, page 6971 and 6972. The protected witness was asked whether he recognised the signature at the bottom and indicated he did not, and the Defence then said that it would like the document, this particular document, to be given an exhibit number and they would authenticate this document in the course of presenting their case. No such evidence has been presented by them in the course of the case in respect of this particular document. That is our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, a priori, it cannot be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have two propositions for the Court. One involves something that the witness said, but I think this was in a closed session, and I think we better go into a private is session for just a moment while I quote a passage of the transcript relating to this issue. Just for a moment, Mr. President. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: at 12.20 p.m., to be reconvened on, Monday, the 5th day of July, 1999 at 2 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: pages 24300 to 24367 redacted – in private session
